Both the 1860 and 1880 Salt Lake County census records have been confidently matched to the Pratt family in the tree. The 1860 census shows Joseph (age 38, born England), his wife Ann (35), daughter Sarah (13), and son Joseph Jr. (10) all living in Salt Lake County — names, birth years, and birthplaces match the tree exactly, and the family traveled the well-documented Latter-day Saint emigration route from Great Britain to Utah. Twenty years later the 1880 census finds Joseph (now 58) and Ann (55) still in Salt Lake County with their son Joseph Jr. (30) still at home; Sarah is gone from the household by then, which is expected for a woman in her early thirties who would likely have married and moved to her own home. The FamilySearch similarity scores for all seven personas came in at 0.78, solidly in the confident range, and no conflicts emerged between the two records or with anything already in the tree.

The natural next step is to search for Sarah Pratt's marriage record, since she appears in 1860 but not 1880 — finding her would extend the family picture and confirm she simply married out rather than died young.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

**Why `speculative` and not `probable`**

The system has two other Hermann Gaetjens formally recorded as namesakes of I1: ns_001 (Hermann Conrad Gaetjen, b. 28 Aug 1873, d. 12 Jan 1957, San Francisco) and ns_002 (Herman Gaetjen, b. 1827, d. 9 Oct 1899, Butte County). Both records are single-person — there is no spouse, parent, or child of I1 who appears in either source that could act as a tie assertion and lift the cap. The qualitative assessment for the Great Register is genuinely Moderate (score 0.43, same city, distinctive surname variant, both namesakes independently excludable on age), and the Germans to America record is Moderate on qualitative grounds with its very low score (0.006) entirely attributable to the birth year conflict between the record's 1854 and I1's unsourced ~1859 estimate. Without the namesake cap, the Great Register would support `probable`.

**What you can do to lift the cap.** The cap lifts the moment a source is found that ties the record to I1 specifically rather than to either namesake. The clearest candidates:
- A census record (1880, 1900) showing Hermann Gaetjen at the right age with wife Amelia Nichols and the two known children. A family census entry would let the children and spouse serve as tie assertions at `probable`, immediately elevating the Great Register and passenger index links.
- The 1875 naturalization record itself (California County Naturalizations, FamilySearch collection 2125028) may give a more specific German birthplace and could name an older relative or witness.
- San Francisco city directories for 1875–1878 may show a fireman named Gatjen/Gaetjen at 5 Cook Street, which could be cross-matched.

Both records were tentatively matched to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) — the 1875 San Francisco voter registration (naming Hermann Gatjen, age 21, a fireman from Germany, naturalized that same day) and a passenger index entry (Herm Gaetjen, born 1854 in Prussia, arrived New York 2 June 1871). The evidence is promising: the surname is an uncommon Low German form, both records give the same birth year of about 1854, the other two Hermann Gaetjens in California are ruled out by age (one born in 1873 was not yet alive in 1871; one born in 1827 was far too old), and a man naturalized in San Francisco in 1875 is exactly who you would expect to be fathering children there from 1878 onward. However, because two namesakes are formally registered, the system requires a source that also names his wife Amelia or one of the children before it will accept these as "probably" rather than "only possibly" his records. The next step is to search for a census record — ideally the 1880 federal census — that shows Hermann with Amelia and the children in San Francisco, which would tie both records firmly to him.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The person-evidence agent reviewed assertion **a_001** (the 1875 census "Anders Pedersen" record) against tree person **Anders Hansen (I1)** and found a **weak match** that cannot be auto-linked. Here is its full assessment:

---

**Points of agreement:**
- Given name "Anders" — exact match
- Birth year ~1868 (age 7 in 1875) — exact match
- Birthplace Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway — matches

**Core identifier conflict:**
- The surname **"Pedersen"** is a 1875-active Norwegian patronymic meaning *son of Peder*. Your subject's father is **Hans Olsen**, whose children would carry the patronymic **"Hansen"** — a completely different name. In 1875 Norway, the patronymic system was still fully in use (fixed surnames didn't become law until 1923), so this is not a spelling variant — it names a *different* father.

**Similarity score:** 0.82 (high), but the core identifier conflict caps the match confidence at `speculative`.

**Possible explanations:**
1. Enumerator error in the census
2. The child was living with a stepfather or godfather named Peder and enumerated under his name
3. This is a *different* child named Anders, born in the same place and year

---

**Your decision is needed:** The agent is waiting for your confirmation before creating any link. Two options:

- **Create a `speculative` link** from a_001 to Anders Hansen (I1), documenting the patronymic conflict in the rationale
- **No link** — treat this as a different person

What would you like to do?

**Naming customs finding (Norway, 1875):** The FamilySearch Norway naming page confirms that during 1875, patronymic surnames were still the norm. Fixed surnames only began to be adopted "during the end of the 19th century," and the first naming law was not passed until 1923. This means "Pedersen" in 1875 was an active patronymic — it means "son of Peder." The subject's known father is Hans Olsen, which would produce the patronymic "Hansen," not "Pedersen." These are different words naming different fathers.

**Same-person score:** 0.82 (strong band), matched: true.

---

**Correlation assessment — agreement vs. conflict:**

Points of agreement:
- Given name "Anders" matches exactly
- Birth year ~1868 matches exactly (age 7 in 1875)
- Birthplace Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway matches the project objective's stated birthplace

Core identifier conflict:
- Surname "Pedersen" is a 1875-active patronymic meaning "son of Peder." The subject's father is Hans Olsen, whose children would bear the patronymic "Hansen." These names explicitly identify different fathers. The naming customs page confirms the patronymic system was in full use in 1875 and does not support treating this as a fixed-surname variant.

**Match threshold determination:** Per the GPS match policy, a differing patronymic names a different father, and is a core identifier conflict, regardless of the same-person score. A 0.82 score does not auto-link past a conflict. The match strength is **Weak** (core identifier conflicts), capped at `speculative`. This requires a pause for your confirmation before any link is created.

---

This is a weak match. The evidence agrees on the given name "Anders," birth year ~1868, and Ringsaker, Hedmark, Norway — all strong convergences. However, the surname "Pedersen" (son of Peder) directly contradicts the expected patronymic "Hansen" (son of Hans, the subject's known father). In 1875 Norway, this surname difference was not a spelling variant — it named a different father. Possible explanations include enumerator error, the child living with a step-father or godfather named Peder, or this being a different child named Anders born in the same place and year.

**Do you want me to create a `speculative` link (pe_ entry) from a_001 and a_002 to Anders Hansen (I1), documenting the patronymic conflict in the rationale? Or do you believe this is a different person and no link should be created?**

---

The 1875 Norwegian census lists an "Anders Pedersen," age 7, born in Ringsaker, Hedmark — a child who matches your subject in given name, birth year, and hometown, producing a high similarity score of 0.82. Despite that, the surname "Pedersen" means "son of Peder," whereas your Anders Hansen's father was Hans Olsen, whose children would carry the surname "Hansen." In 1875 Norway, surnames were still patronymic and actively named the father, so this is a genuine discrepancy, not just a spelling difference. Whether this is a census error, a different child, or something like the boy being enumerated with a stepfather is unclear — your call is needed before any link is recorded.

No fabricated material; all claims are grounded in the tool responses and the before-state.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments

No calls landed in fixture_not_found; all matched successfully. The skill recovered cleanly from a validation rejection on the first research_append batch (missing same_person scores for a_019 and a_020) by calling same_person for those assertions and resubmitting.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: All 22 person_evidence entries correctly use 'probable' confidence. The skill applied the decided rule: an unexplained move outside the residence cluster (Horsham, Sussex to Maury, Tennessee, 6,804 km, no documentary bridge or corridor) caps the link at probable, never confident. The match_score of 0.78 (strong band on name, age, household composition, and internal consistency across two censuses) does not override the geographic cap. No entry claims confident; no entry treats the move as a contradiction or speculative. The rationales consistently cite the geographic gap as the reason for the cap.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each rationale cites multiple specific matching attributes: name (exact match 'William Weller', 'Mary Weller', etc.), age (consistent with ~1825, ~1828, ~1852, ~1855, ~1859 birth years), location (Maury, Tennessee, 1870 and 1880), family context (head with wife Mary and children James, Ellen, George; household position consistent with son/daughter roles), and English birthplace. Rationales explicitly name the geographic gap: 'Maury, Tennessee, 1870 vs England: outside, 6,804 km; no corridor or bridge.' The skill addresses why the link is probable rather than confident by citing the unexplained trans-Atlantic move. Competing candidates are not explicitly ruled out in text, but the exact name and household composition match across two independent censuses, combined with the geographic cap, implicitly addresses disambiguation.

dimensions.name: Multi-person awareness
dimensions.rationale: Relationship assertions in the 1880 census (a_019: 'Wife of William Weller'; a_020: 'Son of William Weller') were linked to both parties. a_019 produced pe_017 (I2 as wife) and pe_018 (I1 as husband). a_020 produced pe_021 (I5 as son) and pe_022 (I1 as father). Both sides of each relationship are represented in person_evidence, satisfying the cardinality requirement.

dimensions.name: Person minting and connecting edges
dimensions.rationale: No new persons were minted; all five persons (I1–I5) already existed in the tree. The skill correctly linked assertions to existing persons via person_evidence and materialized facts via materialize_facts, which enriched the existing persons with sourced facts from the census records. No edges were written via tree_edit add_relationship because the existing ParentChild and Couple relationships were already in the tree (R1–R7 on file before this run). The skill correctly noted this: 'All existing ParentChild (I1/I2 → I3, I4, I5) and Couple (I1 ↔ I2) edges were already in the tree; no new edges written.' For a household record (census), edges are owed only when the record establishes a new relationship; here, all relationships were pre-existing, so not writing new edges is correct.

dimensions.name: Score discipline
dimensions.rationale: same_person was called for every assertion linked to a tree candidate. For the 1870 census, calls were made for a_001 (I1), a_003 (I2), a_005 (I3), a_007 (I4), a_009 (I5). For the 1880 census, calls were made for a_012 (I1), a_014 (I2), a_016 (I5), a_019 (I1 with recordRole=head for the second party), and a_020 (I1 with recordRole=head for the second party). Each score (0.78) was recorded in match_score and informed the confidence decision (capped at probable by the geographic gap, not elevated by the score). The score was treated as input that informs, not replaces, the correlation analysis.
